Abstract: Ti-silicates activate H2O2 to form Ti-hydroperoxo and Ti-peroxo intermediates that can react with alkenes to form epoxide products. Comparisons of kinetics for 1-octene epoxidation with H2O2 on Ti- BEA and Ti-MFI catalysts with different hydrophilicities in methanol (CH3OH) or acetonitrile (CH3CN) solvents show the significance of the solvent for stabilizing catalytically-relevant species and the complex interdependencies between solvent, catalyst topology, and hydrophilicity. Epoxidation turnover rates are higher in CH3CN than CH3OH for Ti-BEA, but the opposite trend is observed for Ti-MFI. Ti-silicates with greater silanol densities, however, give greater epoxidation turnover rates than their hydrophobic counterparts in both solvents. Kinetic, spectroscopic, and thermodynamic analyses show that differences in turnover rates mainly arise from changes in the stabilization of reactive surface species by solvent mediated interactions, because the mechanism of the reaction and stability of the fluid-phase reactants remain similar in CH3CN and CH3OH. Specifically, apparent activation free energy values (Δ ‡ ) indicate that surface intermediates responsible for alkene epoxidation are stabilized to a greater

extent in CH3CN on Ti-BEA and in CH3OH on Ti-MFI. Hydrophilic Ti-silicates present lower Δ ‡ values regardless of solvent identity, which suggests that these differences correspond to the number of hydrogen-bonding solvent molecules found near reactive species bound to Ti active sites. Taken together, these findings demonstrate the role of solvent molecules in allowing reactive intermediates to recognize the properties of active sites beyond the length-scale of covalent bonds, which carry implications for epoxidation but also other reactions within solvent-filled pores of microporous materials.

## 1. Introduction

Zeolites are microporous, crystalline materials used as catalysts and adsorbents [1,2]. Rates and selectivities for chemical transformations depend strongly upon the stabilization of reactive intermediates and transition states within the sub-nanometer pores of zeolites [3–11]. The extent of stabilization depends on the dispersive forces between the confined molecules and the surrounding pore walls, which influence activation free energy barriers and consequently dictate chemical reaction rates [12]. Thus, the rational design of improved catalysts and adsorbents rely on modifying the environment of zeolite pores to introduce favorable interactions at the active site. For instance, systematic changes in the number of silanol groups or degree of hydrophobicity within zeolitic materials can impact turnover rates of glucose isomerization [13,14], structure of confined polar solvents [15], selective adsorption in solvent mixtures [16,17], and effect of liquid water on intrinsic activity and framework stability [18–20]. Separately, tetravalent transition metal atoms (e.g., Ti and Sn) can be deposited onto or substituted into zeolite frameworks to form catalysts for olefin epoxidation and Baeyer-Villiger oxidation reactions [21]. Framework Ti atoms in BEA results in stronger Lewis acid active sites, more electrophilic reactive intermediates (i.e., metal-hydroperoxide (M-OOH) or metal-peroxo (M-(η2-O2))), and consequently greater turnover rates for epoxidations than comparable Nb- and Ta-BEA catalysts [22]. The varied forms of interactions within micropores of zeolites offer multiple opportunities to increase turnover rates and selectivities for reactions significant for production of chemicals and fuels, and these gains reduce the energy requirements and carbon footprint of large-scale chemical production processes [23]. Comparisons of alkene epoxidations over titanosilicates demonstrate that variations in the pore structure [24], the solvent identity [25], and the reactant [26,27] influence catalytic rates and selectivities. The hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) – propylene oxide (HPPO) process achieves the epoxidation of propylene with H2O2 and gives high yields over Ti-MFI catalysts in aqueous solutions of methanol (CH3OH) [28–30] , while other work indicates that Ti-MWW materials in aqueous acetonitrile (CH3CN) catalyze this reaction at greater rates and equal or better selectivities [31–33]. The reasons for these differences are not clear. Prior research on alkene epoxidations (C3 – C8) over titanosilicates have consistently shown that the greatest turnover rates occur in CH3OH solvent for Ti-MFI materials [34–37]. In contrast, selected results from a limited set of conditions show that Ti-BEA, a material with slightly larger pore diameter (~0.6 nm) than Ti-MFI (~0.55 nm), gives greater alkene epoxidation turnover rates in CH3CN than in CH3OH for longer chain linear alkenes (i.e., 1-hexene and 1-octene (C8H16)) [38–40]. Several hypotheses were proposed to explain the distinction between turnover rates in different solvents. The most commonly proposed explanation suggests that solvent molecules coordinate to Ti active sites, actively participate in the reaction, and influence the intrinsic reactivity of the Ti atoms; however, the mechanisms and nature of these interactions remains debated [41,42]. Another common explanation attributes these differences to a confluence of rates of intrapore diffusion of reactants and products and equilibrium uptakes that depend on the solvent present within the micropores of Ti-zeolites [36,43]. Adsorption isotherm experiments indicate that 1-hexene concentrations within Ti-MFI are greater in CH3OH than in CH3CN but the results were insufficient to demonstrate that these variations fully account for differences between turnover rates within different solvents [36]. These findings illustrate the complexity of solvent-derived effects and propose multiple plausible hypotheses, but the factors responsible for the large differences in rates between Tizeolites with distinct topologies and the reasons for the specific pairing between topologies and solvents remain unclear. Recent contributions demonstrate the importance of solvent structure and reorganization on regulating catalytic reactions within pores of zeolites that contain molecules bound to active sites but also with consequential densities of fluid-like molecules (e.g., reactant, product, or solvent molecules). Our group has shown that the presence of small amounts of H2O molecules in solvents, such as CH3CN, has significant effects on turnover rates and selectivities of alkene epoxidations, and the magnitude of these effects depend on the density of silanol defects. In aqueous CH3CN, hydrophilic Ti-BEA samples that possess ~5 silanol nests ((SiOH)4) per unit cell give turnover rates for 1-octene epoxidation 100-fold faster

than hydrophobic Ti-BEA materials that possess ~0 silanol nests ((SiOH)4) per unit cell and do so without a concomitant rise in undesired H2O2 decomposition rates [44]. These differences reflect the perturbation of hydrogen-bond clusters of H2O molecules stabilized near silanol defects by the formation of epoxidation transition states and the entropic gains associated with these disturbances [44–46]. The differences between activation enthalpies and entropies for epoxidation in distinct Ti zeolite topologies and for alkenes of increasing length (C6 – C10) strongly correlates with independent assessments of the molar enthalpies and entropies of hydrogen-bonded water molecules obtained by in situ infrared spectroscopy [46] , which gives compelling evidence that these changes originate from solvent reorganization. Solvent mediated recognition of pore topologies and polarities for alkene epoxidations resemble processes described by others for other catalytic reactions within both Lewis acidic and Bronsted acidic zeolite catalysts. Lercher and co-workers showed that hydronium ions confined within H-BEA enhances liquid-phase cyclohexanol dehydration by an order of magnitude compared to hydronium ions in bulk H2O, due to an increase in the amount of hydronium ions associated with cyclohexanol and greater increase in entropy upon activation within the pores of H-BEA [47]. Cordon et al. studied glucose isomerization on Ti-BEA of different hydrophilicity and reported initial glucose isomerization rates that were ~6 times lower on hydrophilic Ti- BEA-OH than hydrophobic Ti-BEA-F, due to the formation of water structures within hydrophilic voids that reduce the entropy of the isomerization transition state [48]. Bates et al. examined alcohol dehydration reactions within pores of aluminosilicate zeolites and showed that variations in densities of proton sites within H-BEA and differences in zeolite framework (e.g., BEA, MFI, TON) influence the extent to which the dehydration transition states disrupt and reorganize hydrogen-bonded H2O networks [49]. These differences impact rates of ethanol dehydration as the transition states are solvated less effectively and destabilized in the presence of these water networks. Di Iorio et al. reported that turnover rates of the transfer hydrogenation reaction of cyclohexanone with 2-butanol within hydrophobic Sn-BEA were 10 times greater than for hydrophilic analogs [50], which were attributed to excess contributions derived from solvent reorganization within the pores consistent with prior work. These studies demonstrate that sensible choice of zeolite pore architecture can have a large impact on the extent of reactive intermediate and transition state solvation within the reaction environment. In the context of alkene epoxidation, however, it is not well understood how differences in both solvent identity (e.g., CH3CN versus CH3OH) and pore size (e.g., for MFI and BEA) lead to quantitative changes in the free energy of activation. Here, we show that rates of 1-octene epoxidation with H2O2 depend on the identity of the solvent (i.e., CH3CN or CH3OH), the density of internal SiOH groups (used interchangeably with pore hydrophilicity), and the zeolite topology (Ti-BEA or Ti-MFI) in ways that can be explained by differences in the excess free energy of solvated transition state complexes. Epoxidation rates for hydrophilic Ti-BEA-OH are 20× higher in CH3CN than in CH3OH, while epoxidation rates for hydrophilic Ti-MFI-OH are 1.4× greater in CH3OH than in CH3CN. When comparing Ti-silicates of similar framework but different silanol densities, hydrophilic variants of Ti-BEA and Ti-MFI (i.e., Ti-BEA-OH and Ti-MFI-OH) give epoxidation turnover rates that are significantly higher than their hydrophobic counterparts (i.e., Ti-BEA-F and Ti-MFI-F) in both CH3OH and CH3CN solvents. The large differences in turnover rates do not correspond to changes in the identity of active intermediates or the mechanism for epoxidation, neither of which varies in a significant manner with solvent identity, silanol density, or framework. Instead, the differences in turnover rates reflect the different extent of stabilization provided by interactions between the transition states for epoxidation, the solvent molecules, and nearby silanol nests, which collectively determine excess contributions to the apparent Gibbs free energy of activation (Δ ‡ ). Δ ‡ decreases with increasing silanol density (or hydrophilicity) regardless of solvent identity and framework type, which aligns with higher epoxidation turnover rates obtained on more hydrophilic Ti-silicates. Differences between Δ ‡ among the combinations of CH3CN or CH3OH solvents with Ti-BEA or Ti-MFI catalysts show that the small differences between the dimensions of 10-membered rings of MFI compared to the 12-membered rings of BEA significantly influence the organization, stability, and dynamics of solvent molecules within these pores. These observations suggest that the differences do not appear to derive from specific interactions between solvents and framework Ti atom. Collectively, the data shown in this study show how

Materials and Methods 2.1. Synthesis of Ti-BEA and Ti-MFI Materials. All Ti-BEA (except Ti-BEA-250B; Si/Al ratio = 250) and Ti-MFI were previously synthesized and characterized [44,46,51]. Here, we denote materials with the *BEA and MFI topology as BEA and MFI, respectively, for clarity. Ti-BEA-250B is equivalent to Ti-BEA-250A synthesized in a prior study [44] but from a more recent synthesis batch. Relevant characterization data and procedures are summarized here and in the Supporting Information section. Table 1 displays the source, initial Si/Al ratio, Ti loading, and micropore volume of the catalysts. Post-synthetic modification methods were used to form Ti-BEA-OH (Si/Al ratio = 12.5), Ti-BEA-75A (Si/Al ratio = 75), and Ti-BEA-250B from commercially available Al-BEA samples. Al-BEA was first treated with concentrated HNO3 (Macron Chemicals, 68-70 wt.%, 20 cm3 g-1) under reflux for 18 h to remove aluminum atoms in the framework through formation of soluble Al(NO3)3. The dealuminated BEA was then recovered through vacuum filtration and rinsed with deionized H2O (17.8 MΩ·cm, 50 cm3 g-1). The recovered solids were subsequently dried in a horizontal furnace for 6 h at 823 K (5 K min-1) under a continuous flow of air (Airgas, Ultra-zero grade; 100 cm3 min-1) to form Si-BEA. The Si-BEA synthesized possessed Si/Al ratios >1400, determined from energy dispersive X-ray fluorescence (EDXRF). Ti atoms were incorporated into Si-BEA by combining a stirred suspension of Si-BEA in dichloromethane (Fisher Chemicals, ACS grade; ~20 cm3 min-1) with an appropriate amount of TiCl4 (Sigma-Aldrich, 99.9%) at reflux. Over the course of 4 h, the suspension turned from white in color to light brown. The volatile components were removed via rotary evaporation to yield off-white solids, which were then treated at 823 K for 6 h (5 K min-1) in flowing air (100 cm3 min-1) to yield bright white Ti-BEA.

IR spectra were collected with a custom-built temperature-controlled transmission cell coupled to a Fourier transform infrared spectrometer (Bruker, Tensor 37) equipped with a liquid nitrogen cooled HgCdTe detector. Approximately 50 mg of the catalysts were pressed into pellets with a hydraulic press (Carver, Model C) and transferred to the transmission cell. CaF2 windows were subsequently loaded onto the transmission cell and the transmission cell was connected to a gas manifold. Catalysts were heated to 573 K at 10 K min-1 and held for at least 3 h in flowing He (50 cm3 min-1) to desorb water and volatile compounds. IR spectra (128 scans, 1 cm-1 resolution) of a given catalyst were then collected with respect to the background spectra obtained without the catalyst wafer in the transmission cell. 2.3. Rate Measurements for Epoxide Formation and H2O2 Decomposition. The rates of C8H16 epoxidation were measured within batch reactors (100 cm3, three-necked roundbottomed flasks) attached to reflux condensers to minimize solvent loss by evaporation. C8H16 (Sigma- Aldrich, 98%) and H2O2 (Fisher Chemicals, 30 wt.% in H2O) reactants were added to a solution of CH3OH (Fisher Chemicals, HPLC grade) or CH3CN (Fisher Chemicals, HPLC grade) with benzene (~5 µL; Sigma-Aldrich, thiophene-free, >99%), which served as an internal standard for compositional analysis by gas chromatography. The solution was heated to the desired temperature (303 – 333 K), while stirring at 700 rpm. The epoxidation reactions were initiated by the addition of Ti-catalysts into the solution. Small aliquots (~500 µL) of the reaction solution were extracted with a 1 mL syringe through a syringe filter (0.22 µm, polypropylene) at different time points. The concentrations of the organic components were then measured with a gas chromatograph (Agilent, 6850) equipped with a flame-ionization detector and liquid autosampler (CTC Analytics, GC Pal). The different species present in the gas chromatography were identified and quantified using retention times and response factors obtained from standard solutions of known concentration. The H2O2 decomposition rates were also measured in batch reactors, but these rates were measured in solutions of H2O2 and CH3OH or CH3CN (i.e., in the absence of 1-octene and benzene). The concentration of H2O2 in each aliquot was determined by colorimetric titration with an aqueous solution of CuSO4 (8.3 mM, Fisher Chemicals, >98.6%), neocuproine (12 mM, Sigma-Aldrich, >98%), and ethanol (25% v/v, Decon Laboratories, 100%). The titrated solutions were measured with a spectrophotometer (Spectronic, 20 Genesys) at 454 nm, and the absorbances were compared to calibrated standards to determine the H2O2 concentration as a function of time.

Normalization by the peak area of ν(Si-O-Si) overtones provides a basis for comparison among samples of a given topology, because the absorbance of ν(Si-O-Si) overtones scales in proportion to the quantity of a given material. Table 2 shows that values of ΦIR increase as initial Si/Al ratio of the parent Si- BEA decreases. Ti-BEA with lower Si/Al ratio were previously determined to have higher density of (SiOH)x groups (from 29Si solid-state MAS NMR spectroscopy) [44]. Thus, ΦIR values can be used to correlate the density of (SiOH)x groups within Ti-BEA materials, where the highest ΦIR value correspond to highest number of crystal defects (SiOH)x groups among Ti-BEA materials in this study. This semiquantitative method to determine density of (SiOH)x groups can also be applied to zeolites of other topologies (e.g., MFI and FAU), as the characteristic vibrational features obtained from infrared spectra are similar among titanosilicates [51,63]. However, comparison of ΦIR values between zeolites of different frameworks (e.g., between Ti-BEA and Ti-MFI) cannot be directly made as the extinction coefficient for the ν(Si-O-Si) overtones may differ between frameworks. Ti-MFI-OH synthesized in hydroxide media has a ΦIR value two orders of magnitude greater than Ti-MFI-F synthesized in fluoride media (Ti-MFI-F), which shows that Ti-MFI-OH contains higher density of (SiOH)x group compared to Ti-MFI-F, and is consistent with the fact that Ti-MFI synthesized in fluoride media is more hydrophobic than Ti-MFI synthesized in hydroxide media [38]. This work expands a series of publications from our group [22,27,44,63–65,68] and others [47– 50,77,78] that examine how variations in zeolite pore architecture and its interactions with solvent molecules affect turnover rates and selectivities for liquid phase catalytic reactions. Previous studies on solvent effects in liquid-phase alkene epoxidation reactions have typically associated solvent effects of epoxidation reactions on differences in intraporous alkene concentrations [36,43] and at times intraparticle concentration gradients or diffusion limitations. Here, kinetic measurements show clear differences between epoxidation turnover rates and barriers obtained in different solvents under conditions that rigorously demonstrate an absence of diffusion limitations, ensure identical kinetically relevant steps, and lead to the saturation of Ti active sites by Ti-OOH intermediates. Application of transition state theory to interpret the differences between turnover rates in different solvents and zeolites with distinct topology suggest that changes in Δ ‡ values are responsible for the differences in rates and possess a complex functional dependence on the solvent identity, zeolite topology, and silanol density. Systematic elimination of two parameters (i.e., ΔQRS  and Δ	WX ‡ ) that contribute to Δ ‡ reveals that only ΔUV  leads to

significant changes in Δ ‡ . The physical interpretation of this effect seems intuitive: as an alkene enters pores and approaches Ti-OOH intermediates solvent molecules must reorganize to accommodate the alkene and the enthalpic and entropic changes associated with reorganization will reflect the interactions among solvent molecules, pore walls, and reactive intermediates. The elimination of Δ	WX ‡ , based on results from our prior studies [22,27,64,65,68], implies that solvent molecules weakly coordinate to the active site under conditions where Ti-OOH dominates. Therefore, the influence of solvent molecules and their impact on Δ ‡ most likely takes the form of excess contribution (or second coordination sphere effects). Taken together, these findings suggest that differences in rates result from the enthalpic and entropic costs associated with disruption of hydrogen-bonding interactions among solvent molecules during the adsorption of 1-octene into the pores. The different pore topology and pore hydrophilicity undoubtedly lead to distinct structures of solvent molecules within the pores. However, atomistically detailed descriptions of the solvent structures require coordinated experimental and computational analysis that includes quantitative touchstones. This work demonstrates the nuanced contributions of solvent structures towards epoxidation reactions within the micropores of zeolite and highlights the complexity and importance of understanding the intertwined relationship of solvent structure, pore sizes, and pore hydrophilicity.

4. Conclusion. The turnover rates for epoxidation depend strongly on the type of solvents, zeolite topology and the density of silanol groups in a complex manner that eluded prior explanations. In general, turnover rates of epoxidation increase with higher (SiOH)x densities for both Ti-BEA and Ti-MFI catalysts, regardless of solvent identity. When solvent identity is the only variable, trends in turnover rates are different on Ti-BEA than on Ti-MFI. Specifically, within all Ti-BEA materials, turnover rates are higher in CH3CN than CH3OH; however, Ti-MFI gives greater turnover rates in CH3OH than CH3CN though the span of these differences are less than within Ti-BEA. The observed differences in turnover rates do not stem from the differences in the proposed elementary steps, electronic identities, and properties of reactive intermediates, which remain functionally indistinguishable among the materials studied. Instead, the observed differences in turnover rates are due to differences in apparent free energies (Δ ‡ ) which arise from interactions among solvent molecules, pore topology, and silanol groups present that influence the stability of epoxidation transition states bound to framework Ti active sites. The differences largely correspond to changes in the solvent structure induced by alkene adsorption near Ti-OOH intermediates and appear in the free energies of adsorption (ΔUV).

Values of Δ ‡ vary with solvent identity and silanol densities of Ti-silicates. In general, higher

epoxidation turnover rates correspond to lower Δ ‡ values (and equivalently more negative ΔUV). For

instance, Δ ‡ values decrease with increasing silanol density in both Ti-BEA and Ti-MFI materials. In

Ti-BEA, values of Δ ‡ are consistently lower by 10 – 12 kJ mol-1 in CH3CN than in CH3OH. Yet Δ ‡ values for Ti-MFI are similar or slightly higher in CH3CN than in CH3OH, and the differences between Δ ‡ in the two solvents are only ~ 4 - 9 kJ mol-1. The smaller gap in ΔΔ ‡ values in Ti-MFI compared to Ti-BEA may reflect the fact that solvents within these 10 membered ring structures deviate more significantly from their equilibrium structure in the fluid phase than in 12 membered rings of *BEA.  In short, the smaller pores of Ti-MFI reduce the number of hydrogen bonds among all solvent molecules more so than Ti-BEA. These comparisons show that stabilization of epoxidation transition states within different solvents can vary between Ti-silicates of different frameworks and silanol densities. Turnover rates and selectivities for catalytic reactions at solid-liquid interfaces depend on many factors beyond the topology of the solid catalyst, and we might anticipate that exceptions can be found for categorical claims based on narrower considerations. In summary, understanding interactions among solvents and pores and their effects on transition states remains important in the selection of catalysts and solvents to facilitate epoxidation and other liquid-phase reactions. ## Heteroatom Substituted Zeolite FAU with Ultralow Al Contents for Liquid-Phase Oxidation Catalysis

Daniel T. Bregante,a Jun Zhi Tan,a Andre Sutrisno,b and David W. Flahertya,*

Heteroatom framework-substituted zeolites are important materials that enable shape- and size-selective catalysis. The efficacy of these materials for desired catalytic reactions depends critically on dispersive interactions between the microporous void of the zeolite and the reactant molecules stabilized within it. Here, we develop a post-synthetic method to synthesize base and transition metal-substituted (Ti, Nb, Ta, and Sn) FAU with ultralow Al contents (Si:Al > 900), which is confirmed using X-ray diffraction, elemental analysis, and N2 volumetric adsorption and 29Si MAS-NMR, DRUV-vis, and IR spectroscopic characterization. Ti-FAU selectively stabilized styrene (C8H8) within its pores during epoxidation with H2O2. Turnover rates for C8H8 epoxidation within Ti-FAU are 2- and 7-fold greater than in analogous Ti-BEA and Ti-SiO2, respectively; yet, turnover rates of H2O2 decomposition are similar for all three materials. Consequently, Ti-FAU gives greater rates and selectivities for this reaction than common Ti-bearing silicates. The mechanism for epoxidation remains constant for all Tisilicates examined (i.e., Ti-FAU, Ti-BEA, and Ti-SiO2). Therefore, the improved performance of Ti-FAU reflects differences in activation free energies for epoxidation that show an enthalpic preference in Ti-FAU relative to Ti-SiO2 and an entropic gain relative to Ti-BEA. These results demonstrate the synthesis of M-FAU with ultralow Al contents are useful for catalytic reactions involving bulky reactants that can not occur in smaller pore zeotype materials (Ti-MFI), that exhibit deactivation due to changes in Ti-atom coordination (e.g., Ti-SiO2), and that are prone to losses catalyzed by residual Brønsted acid sites (e.g., epoxidations, oxidations, and isomerization reactions).

## Introduction

Decades of research1-8 devoted to zeolite and zeotype catalysts have focused on understanding how the unique pore structure of these materials enables size- and shape-selective catalysis. The rates and selectivities toward specific, desired catalytic transformations depends critically on the dispersive interactions between the micropores of the zeolite catalyst and the reactants contained within these spaces.6, 9, 10 These interactions provide a basis to modify rates and selectivities by stabilizing surface intermediates and transition states along reaction coordinates.

Zeolite catalysts that contain framework-substituted Lewis acidic heteroatoms (e.g., Ti, Sn, Nb, Ta) catalyse stereoselective mono- and di-saccharide isomerization,11, 12 aldol condensation,13-15 alcohol dehydration,16, 17 Baeyer-Villiger oxidation,18-20 and alkene epoxidation reactions.18, 21-26 For example, the discovery that Snsubstituted zeolite *BEA (Sn-BEA) activates ketones for Baeyer- Villiger oxidation25 with hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) catalysed a renaissance of work with Sn-BEA for use in other reactions (e.g., glucose isomerization,11, 27 ethanol dehydration16, 17). Titaniumsubstituted silicalite-1 (TS-1) was developed in the 1980’s and has found industrial application as a catalyst for propylene epoxidation with H2O2,26 which inspired the development of subsequent design principles for epoxidation reactions.3, 4, 10, 22-24, 28-31 The presence of Brønsted acid sites (e.g., those formed at framework Al or B atoms)) catalyse secondary reactions that are detrimental to the desired chemistry, even when Al atoms remain in trace quantities (Si:Al = 10 - 150) .32-35 In the context of alkene epoxidation, the desired epoxides formed by primary reaction pathways readily undergo undesirable ring opening hydrolysis over Brønsted acids,36 which decreases yields. Therefore, researchers invested significant effort into developing synthetic methods that avoid forming these deleterious

sites through direct hydrothermal synthesis11, 27, 28 or through the post-synthetic removal of adventitious Al atoms.37-39

The zeolite faujasite (FAU) is an important structure used in 95% of the catalyst market (by mass),40 due to its widespread use in fluid catalytic cracking units. The synthesis of Al-free metal-substituted FAU (M-FAU) materials have not been reported, despite the widespread use of this framework in the oil and gas industries. Current methods for the synthesis of M-FAU either rely on the postsynthetic modification of Al-FAU20, 41-43 or direct hydrothermal synthesis in the presence of AlNaO2.44 For example, Trejda et al. synthesized Nb- and Ta-substituted FAU hydrothermally in the presence of sodium aluminate (needed to crystalize the structure) yet, this approach produced in M-Al-FAU materials with a Si:Al ratio equal to 2.3.44 Methods for the post-synthetic modification of Al-FAU rely on steaming at high temperatures41 or acid treatments20, 42 to partially remove Al from framework positions and create vacant silanol nest ((SiOH)4) defects that can be substituted with the desired metal atoms. In all previous reports, a significant amount of Al (Si:Al ratios = 19 – 150) remains,20, 41-43, 45 which is detrimental for a number of relevant reactions. Consequently, the advent of synthetic methods to produce Al-free M-FAU would be impactful for numerous industrially practiced catalytic reactions including alkene epoxidation and biomass upgrading.

Here, we show that sequential treatments of Al-FAU in concentrated HNO3 removes nearly all of the Al within these materials and increase Si:Al ratios from 15 to values greater than 900. The incorporation of base and early-transition metals into the FAU framework preserves the crystallinity of these materials and is confirmed using a combination of techniques including X-ray diffraction, N2 volumetric adsorption, diffuse-reflectance UV-vis spectroscopy, 29Si nuclear magnetic resonance spectroscopy, and infrared spectroscopy. Infrared spectra of pyridine adsorbed within M-FAU synthesize by these methods show the presence of Lewis acid sites and undetectable numbers of Brønsted acid sites (within the sensitivity of the method).

Comparisons of the rates, selectivities, and yields for styrene (C8H8) epoxidation with H2O2 over Ti-FAU to that in other Ti-silicates demonstrates advantages of locating Ti active sites within the supercages of the FAU structure. Turnover rates for styrene

FAU Dealumination and Heteroatom Incorporation

Heteroatom-substituted FAU (M-FAU) were prepared through the post-synthetic modification of H+-form Al-FAU (Zeolyst, CBV 720; Si:Al ~ 15). Al-FAU was treated in HNO3 (Macron Chemicals, 68 – 70 wt. %, 20 cm3 gAl-FAU-1) at reflux for 18 hours with the intent to remove framework Al by forming soluble Al(NO3)3. The solids were recovered by vacuum filtration, washed with additional HNO3 (5 cm3 gAl-FAU-1), and deionized H2O (17.8 MΩ ∙ cm; 25 cm3 gAl-FAU-1). Note that concentrated HNO3 can easily cause chemical burns and should be handled carefully. These washed solids were then dried at 823 K (5 K min-1) for 6 h in flowing air (Airgas, Ultra-zero grade; 100 cm3 min-1) to produce a partially-dealuminated FAU with a Si:Al of ~200 (estimated by energy dispersive X-ray fluorescence, see below). The partial dealumination may result from the redeposition of Al into the FAU framework during filtration at room temperature. To further remove Al atoms, these dried solids were then subjected to a second dealumination sequence identical to that described above to produce Si-FAU with a Si:Al greater than 900.

Ti and Sn atoms were incorporated into the FAU framework through the liquid-phase grafting of TiCl4 (Sigma-Aldrich, 99.9%) or SnCl4∙5H2O (Sigma-Aldrich, 98%) in dichloromethane (DCM, Fisher Chemicals, Certified ACS Stabilized, 25 cm3 gSi-FAU-1). Nb- and Tasubstituted FAU were prepared by refluxing Nb(OEt)5 (Sigma Aldrich, 99.95%) or Ta(OEt)5 (Sigma-Aldrich, 99.98%) in isopropanol (Fisher Chemical, Optima, 25 cm3 gSi-FAU-1). In all cases, the suspensions containing Si-FAU and MCl4 or M(OEt)5 were kept under an argon atmosphere using standard Schlenk technique for at least 6 h. Prior to introduction of the solvent and the MClx or M(OEt)5 precursor, the Si-FAU was dehydrated at 473 K under vacuum (<5 Pa) for 3 h to

desorb any residual H2O that may hydrolyze the metal precursors. Dehydration of Si-FAU is particularly important when using the TiCl4 precursor, which readily hydrolyzes to form oligomeric and bulk TiOx aggregates. The solvent and other volatile components were removed via rotary evaporation and the recovered solids were heated in flowing air (100 cm3 min-1) to 823 K at 5 K min-1 and held for 6 h to yield bright white-colored solids in all cases.

Titanium substituted BEA (Ti-BEA) and Ti-grafted SiO2 (Ti-SiO2) materials were used within a previous study,23 which presents the detailed chemical and physical characterization of these materials. The titanium silicalite-1 (TS-1) material was synthesized according to the recommended procedure from the International Zeolite Association’s Synthesis Commission to contain 0.3 wt. % Ti.46 The relevant characterization data is presented within the Supporting Information (Section S1).

Briefly, Ti-BEA was prepared by the post-synthetic modification of commercial Al-BEA (Zeolyst, CP814E). Al-BEA was contacted with HNO3 at reflux for 18 h with the intent of forming soluble Al(NO3)3. The solids were recovered by vacuum filtration and washed thoroughly with H2O prior to dehydration at 823 K (6 h; 5 K min-1) in flowing air (100 cm3 min-1), which produced Si-BEA (Si:Al > 1200). Ti atoms were incorporated into Si-BEA through the liquid-phase incorporation of TiCl4 in DCM at reflux. Volatile components were removed via rotary evaporation and recovered solids were treated at 823 K (5 K min-1) for 6 h in flowing air (100 cm3 min-1) to produce Ti- BEA.

Ti-SiO2 was synthesized through the grafting of titanium 1,3- dimethoxy-tert-butylcalix[4]arene (Ti-dmCalix) onto SiO2 (Selecto Scientific, 32 – 62 μm particle size, 5.4 nm pore diameter) through reflux in toluene in  an Ar atmosphere.23 Prior to grafting, SiO2 was dehydroxylated at 573 K under vacuum (<5 Pa) for 10 h to produce isolated SiOH and minimize any Ti-O-Ti oligomer formation. TidmCalix-grafted SiO2 was recovered by vacuum filtration and treated at 823 K (5 K min-1) for 6 h in air (100 cm3 min-1) to produce Ti-SiO2.

TS-1 was synthesized hydrothermally in hydroxide media. In short, 150 mg of titanium (IV) butoxide (TBOT; Sigma-Aldrich, 97%) was dissolved in 27.7 g of tetraethylorthosilicate (TEOS; Sigma- Aldrich, 98%) in a polypropylene container to form a homogeneous solution and was subsequently cooled to 273 K. Separately, a mixture of 28.7 g of  tetrapropylammonium hydroxide (TPAOH; Sachem, 40% in H2O) and 50.5 g of H2O was cooled to 273 K and was slowly added (over ~1 min) to the solution of TBOT and TEOS, which yielded a biphasic mixture. This solution was then warmed to 298 K and stirred for 12 h to produce a homogeneous solution, which indicates complete hydrolysis of the TBOT and TEOS. The cover was then removed to evaporate the ethanol and butanol formed through hydrolysis and produce a solution with the approximate composition of 1 Si : 0.0033 Ti : 0.43 TPAOH : 28.3 H2O. This solution was then loaded into a Teflon-lined stainless-steel autoclave (Parr instruments, 125 cm3) that contained 5% (relative to SiO2 in the gel) TS-1 from a previous synthesis. This autoclave was heated to 443 K while rotating (30 rpm) in a convection oven for 3 days. The resulting solids were recovered by centrifugation, washed with H2O, and dried for 16 h at 373 K. The dried solids were then heated in flowing air (100 cm3 min-1) at 823 K (1 K min-1) for 10 h to produce TS-1.

Figure 1 shows X-ray diffractograms for M-FAU all possess features indicative of the FAU framework. The relative crystallinity for each M-FAU was estimated by taking the ratio of the 10.3o and 6.3o and assuming 100% crystallinity within Al- FAU. Reaction Pathways for Alkene Epoxidation with Hydrogen Peroxide

Zeolites and mesoporous silicates bind reactants by charge transfer at active sites but also permit the selective stabilization of surface intermediates through combinations of van der Waals and specific interactions among the extended zeolite surface, the solvent molecules and the reactive species. The extent of stabilization depends on both the size and shape of the confining pore and the reactive species contained within these spaces. Figure 7 shows turnover rates for styrene (C8H8) epoxidation with hydrogen peroxide (H2O2) are significantly greater on Ti-FAU (1.2 nm supercage) than for Ti-BEA (0.65 nm pore) and Ti-SiO2 (5.4 nm pore) at all reaction conditions examined. Specifically, epoxidation rates over Ti-FAU are greater than Ti-BEA and Ti-SiO2 by factors of 2 and 7, respectively. H2O2 selectivities represent the percent of H2O2 molecules that are consumed by epoxidation reaction pathways and decrease in the same fashion as epoxidation turnover rates between

Ti-FAU (47%), Ti-BEA (30%), and Ti-SiO2 (6%). ## Conclusions

Multiple treatments of Al-FAU (Si:Al = 15) in HNO3 removes nearly all of the Al atoms to produce siliceous FAU (Si:Al >900). These treatments are necessary to remove the adventitious Al atoms, that may act as deleterious sites during zeolite catalysis (e.g., within sugar isomerization, alcohol upgrading, alkene epoxidation), . The liquidphase grafting of metal chlorides and alkoxides leads to the isomorphic substitution of metal (M = Ti, Nb, Ta, Sn) atoms into the framework of FAU. Ti-FAU catalysts efficiently activate H2O2 to form Ti-OOH intermediates that are active for alkene epoxidation. In the case of styrene epoxidation, Ti-FAU possesses rates of epoxidation that are greater than Ti-BEA and Ti-SiO2 by factors of 2 and 7, respectively. Rates of H2O2 decomposition, however, are invariant with the characteristic pore diameter of the Ti-silicate catalyst. Differences in catalysis are not due to differences in the mechanism for epoxidation; yet, reflect differences in the stability of the transition states for C8H8 epoxidation. Specifically, C8H8 epoxidation transition states are enthalpically stabilized within Ti-FAU relative to Ti-SiO2 and also possess greater entropic freedom than within Ti-BEA, which results in the lowest free energies within the bounds of solvent stability. The work presented here serves as an exemplary example for how zeolite framework topology can be chosen to selectively

stabilize desired surface intermediates. The synthetic protocols established here will enable the design of new materials in the quest for the rational development of catalysts.
